paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent updates a model using estimates of the direction in which its objective improves. Much of its theory concerns unbiased estimates, but useful estimates can also be biased. This paper addresses a fragmented literature in which different analyses impose different assumptions, making their results difficult to compare.

The authors map the relationships between existing assumptions and introduce a new set that they prove is weaker than the previous ones. Weaker assumptions expand the situations covered by an analysis. Using this framework, they study biased SGD for both convex and non-convex objectives and obtain advantages over earlier theoretical results.

The paper also gives examples where biased estimates outperform unbiased alternatives, or where an unbiased version is unavailable. Experiments support the theoretical findings. The contribution is therefore both organizational and analytical: it makes existing guarantees easier to relate and provides a broader framework for studying biased updates. The examples establish that bias can be useful, rather than that it is always beneficial.
neurips-2023-a-guide-through-the-zoo-of-.tldr: The paper unifies assumptions for biased SGD and develops a broader theoretical framework covering convex and non-convex optimization.

paragraphs: An online learner continually updates itself as new data arrive, so an attacker can influence the learning process itself. This paper studies attacks that perturb training labels to steer those updates. It treats the attacker’s problem through control theory, focusing on how interventions change the learner’s evolving behavior.

The theoretical analysis uses a teacher-student setup and examines several attack strategies. For simple linear learners, the authors derive analytical results describing the steady state, or eventual behavior of learning. Within this setting, they prove that accuracy undergoes a discontinuous transition once attack strength crosses a critical threshold: the change need not be gradual.

Experiments with more complex architectures and real data support the insights from the simplified analysis. The findings indicate that greedy attacks can be highly efficient, particularly when incoming data arrive in small batches. The significance is that vulnerability depends on the dynamics of continued learning, including how data are presented. The exact transition is established theoretically for the analyzed linear setting, while the broader architectural evidence is empirical.
neurips-2023-attacks-on-online-learners-.tldr: A control-theoretic analysis shows how label attacks can sharply disrupt online learning, with experiments highlighting the efficiency of greedy attacks.

paragraphs: Forecasting a time series involves estimating uncertainty as well as predicting a future value. This paper develops accessible algorithms for uncertainty quantification with formal guarantees. It combines ideas from conformal prediction and control theory to address an online setting, where predictions and observations arrive sequentially and the behavior of errors may change.

The methods prospectively model conformal scores, the quantities used to assess prediction errors within the conformal framework. This allows them to adapt to systematic errors associated with seasonal patterns, trends, and broader distribution shifts. The theoretical contribution also simplifies and strengthens existing analyses of online conformal prediction, providing support for these adaptive procedures.

In experiments forecasting statewide U.S. COVID-19 deaths four weeks ahead, the methods improve coverage over the ensemble forecaster used in official CDC communications. Coverage concerns how often uncertainty sets contain the observed outcomes. Additional experiments address electricity demand, market returns, and temperature using several forecasting model families. The released extensible codebase supports testing across forecasting rules, datasets, and new algorithms.
neurips-2023-conformal-pid-control-for-t.tldr: The paper combines conformal prediction and control theory to adapt time-series uncertainty estimates to systematic errors and changing distributions.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search seeks useful networks by exploring combinations of building blocks. Hierarchical search spaces can express structures at multiple levels, but their design has lacked a common framework and often exposes only limited architectural choices. This paper proposes context-free grammars as a unified way to describe and generate these spaces.

The grammar provides compact construction rules for expressive hierarchical architectures. The resulting spaces are hundreds of orders of magnitude larger than common spaces discussed in the literature. By extending and exploiting grammatical properties, the approach enables search over complete architectures and can encourage regularity. This makes the specification of the search space a central part of the method.

To navigate these enormous spaces, the authors introduce a hierarchical kernel for Bayesian optimization. This supplies the search strategy with a way to account for architectural hierarchy while choosing candidates. Their demonstrations show versatility in defining spaces and indicate that the search strategy can outperform existing NAS approaches. The stated advantage is a demonstrated possibility, rather than a guarantee that every larger grammar-defined space yields a better architecture.
neurips-2023-construction-of-hierarchica.tldr: Context-free grammars define expansive hierarchical architecture spaces, paired with a Bayesian optimization strategy designed to search them efficiently.

paragraphs: Constructive solid geometry represents a shape through combinations of simpler geometric pieces. D²CSG learns compact representations of 3D CAD shapes without supervision, training a neural network to reconstruct shapes through a fixed sequence of operations on quadric primitives. The aim is to recover both the shape and a concise construction describing it.

The network has two complementary branches. A cover branch builds an overall shape, while a residual branch constructs a potentially complicated complement that is subtracted from that cover. Each branch assembles unions of primitive intersections or inverses. The authors prove generality of the representation using these complements, making subtraction a central source of expressive power.

Weight dropout helps remove redundant primitives, improving the compactness of the resulting construction tree. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations show better reconstruction quality, more natural primitives, and compact representations compared with the existing alternatives considered. The reported strengths are especially apparent for complex CAD shapes and shapes with many holes. The method combines an expressive representation with a mechanism for reducing unnecessary geometric components.
neurips-2023-d-2-csg-unsupervised-learni.tldr: D²CSG reconstructs CAD shapes using complementary geometric branches and dropout to produce expressive, compact construction trees.

paragraphs: Geometric representation learning uses spaces such as hyperbolic or spherical geometry to represent data. Its success depends partly on whether the chosen geometry matches the data’s underlying structure. This paper addresses that selection problem, which existing methods often handle through human heuristics that may lead to suboptimal choices.

The proposed method uses a sparse gate to select a subset of candidate spaces for each input point. From a pool of N spaces with different geometries, an input selects K, with K smaller than N. Those selected spaces are combined into a Cartesian product space, and the input is processed using that combination.

This design makes geometry selection specific to individual inputs, allowing different points to use different combinations of spaces. The authors aim to automate alignment between data and geometry with minimal overhead. Experiments on real-world tasks show that the method can make these choices without human intervention and improve performance. The findings support adaptive space selection as a practical way to make better use of geometric representations.
neurips-2023-data-informed-geometric-spa.tldr: A sparse gating mechanism lets each input select and combine geometric spaces, improving alignment between representations and data in experiments.

paragraphs: Distributed optimization can involve workers sending information to a central node after delays, so updates may use stale information. This paper studies that problem for stochastic weakly convex optimization. It improves the understanding of how delay affects convergence and develops algorithms that reduce its influence under the settings analyzed.

For delayed stochastic subgradient descent, the authors obtain a tighter convergence rate governed by expected delay rather than maximum delay. This distinction matters when unusually late messages make the worst case much larger than typical delays. For an important class of composition problems, their delayed stochastic prox-linear method places delay effects only in a higher-order term, which becomes negligible after enough iterations.

The paper also adds a simple safeguarding step to both methods to handle arbitrary delays. With this safeguard, the convergence rates depend on the number of workers rather than delay quantities. Numerical experiments support the proposed methods’ empirical advantages. Together, the results show several ways to reduce the theoretical penalty from stale information, with the strongest conclusions tied to the corresponding algorithm and problem structure.
neurips-2023-delayed-algorithms-for-dist.tldr: The paper sharpens convergence guarantees for delayed distributed optimization and introduces methods that reduce or remove delay dependence from those guarantees.

paragraphs: Cooperative players often coordinate through conventions: shared ways of acting that do not require explicit communication. Standard self-play can settle on an arbitrary convention, leaving an agent poorly prepared for unfamiliar partners. This paper develops a way to learn multiple meaningfully different conventions for collaborative games and human-AI interaction.

Training rewards agents for successful self-play while reducing their rewards when paired with previously discovered conventions. This cross-play objective encourages new conventions to differ in how coordination works. Because deliberately poor cross-play could encourage uncooperative behavior, the authors introduce mixed-play. It creates initial states through mixtures of self-play and cross-play transitions, then trains agents to maximize self-play reward from those states.

Mixed-play is intended to preserve good-faith behavior despite the adversarial part of the diversity objective. Evaluations across collaborative games, including Overcooked, find that the technique can adapt to human conventions. When paired with real users, it surpasses human-level performance in the reported evaluations. The findings connect convention diversity during training with better coordination with human partners.
neurips-2023-diverse-conventions-for-hum.tldr: The method learns diverse cooperative conventions and uses mixed-play to support good-faith coordination, improving collaboration with humans in evaluations.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks a model to recognize inputs that fall outside its familiar data distribution. Outlier exposure helps by training with auxiliary examples of unfamiliar inputs. This paper addresses a practical difficulty: collecting enough representative outliers to cover the boundary between familiar and unfamiliar data can be challenging.

Diversified Outlier Exposure, or DivOE, expands the usefulness of the outliers already available. It introduces a training objective that explicitly synthesizes informative outliers, diversifying the auxiliary distribution. A multi-step optimization procedure generates examples beyond the original collection, providing extrapolated training material rather than relying entirely on the coverage of collected outliers.

The framework is compatible with many variants of outlier exposure, so its central contribution is a way to enrich their training signal. Extensive experiments and analyses characterize the approach and support its effectiveness for OOD detection. The stated finding is that informative extrapolation improves the use of auxiliary outliers; it does not establish that a finite synthetic collection covers every possible unfamiliar input.
neurips-2023-diversified-outlier-exposur.tldr: DivOE synthesizes informative new outliers from available examples to improve out-of-distribution detection.

paragraphs: In a generative adversarial network, the discriminator helps train the generator by learning to distinguish real and generated data. The generated distribution changes throughout training, creating a moving target. This paper examines that difficulty through online continual learning, treating generated examples as an evolving stream that the discriminator must keep learning from.

The authors observe that learning from earlier generated data can slow the discriminator’s adaptation to newly generated data. That slowdown can reduce the quality of generated outputs. Their method detects when the discriminator is becoming slow to learn new information and responds by dynamically masking its features, explicitly encouraging faster adaptation.

The resulting discriminator adjusts its feature masking as training progresses so that it can track the changing generated distribution. Experiments report better performance than the state-of-the-art approaches considered. The contribution is a mechanism for responding to an observed learning slowdown inside GAN training. Its motivation connects the quality of generated results to how well the discriminator keeps up with the generator’s changing behavior.
neurips-2023-dynamically-masked-discrimi.tldr: A discriminator that detects adaptation slowdowns and dynamically masks features improves GAN results in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Voting offers a way to make collective decisions whose procedure stakeholders can understand. Randomized voting rules can improve decision efficiency, but complicated randomization may make the procedure difficult to explain. This paper asks how much of that efficiency benefit is available when randomness is introduced through a simple, understandable step.

The authors study rules that add simple randomization to a deterministic voting procedure. They focus on two families: randomized positional scoring rules and random committee member rules. Their notion of efficiency comes from the distortion framework, which evaluates the quality of voting outcomes. Here, efficiency concerns decision quality rather than merely the time needed to compute a result.

Both theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation show that these families can achieve explainability and efficiency together to some extent. That qualification matters: the paper investigates attainable gains within deliberately simple rule families. Its contribution is to make the complexity of the decision procedure part of the design problem, alongside the quality of the decisions it produces.
neurips-2023-explainable-and-efficient-r.tldr: Simple randomization can improve voting efficiency while retaining explainability, as shown for two families of voting rules.

paragraphs: Some questions about images require external knowledge as well as visual understanding. Retrieval-augmented visual question answering first retrieves relevant documents and then uses them to answer. This paper improves that retrieval stage, addressing information lost when images are converted to text and fine details missed by coarse query-document representations.

Fine-grained Late-interaction Multi-modal Retrieval, or FLMR, adds visual representations that complement the image-to-text descriptions. A simple alignment network connects a vision model to an existing text retriever. The method also represents images and questions with multi-dimensional embeddings, allowing the comparison with documents to capture finer-grained similarities that the original representation may overlook.

FLMR improves the original retriever’s PRRecall@5 by approximately 8%, according to the reported evaluation. The authors also combine RA-VQA with two state-of-the-art multimodal or language models and achieve roughly a 62% VQA score on OK-VQA. These results address both retrieval and downstream answering: the retrieval method finds more useful knowledge, while the expanded answering system demonstrates performance on knowledge-based visual questions.
neurips-2023-fine-grained-late-interacti.tldr: FLMR combines complementary visual features with fine-grained retrieval representations to improve knowledge retrieval for visual question answering.

paragraphs: Neural networks learn patterns from data, while symbolic solvers reason with explicitly stated mathematical knowledge. SMTLayer connects these capabilities by inserting a Satisfiability Modulo Theories solver into a deep network layer. Domain knowledge is expressed as formulas that participate in both producing an inference and shaping what the network learns.

During the forward pass, the solver combines symbols supplied by earlier layers with the formulas to construct an inference. During the backward pass, information from the solver guides network updates toward representations compatible with the symbolic theory. The solver itself does not need to be differentiable, which is a key feature of the integration.

The authors implement the layer as a PyTorch module. Their experiments show models requiring fewer training samples than conventional models, robustness to certain types of covariate shift, and learned representations consistent with symbolic knowledge. That consistency provides a basis for interpretation through the encoded formulas. The reported robustness applies to particular distribution changes studied, while the broader contribution is an interface between learned representations and explicit reasoning.
neurips-2023-grounding-neural-inference-.tldr: SMTLayer integrates symbolic solvers into neural inference and training, with empirical gains in sample efficiency, selected robustness settings, and interpretability.

paragraphs: Planning through learned subgoals can make a complex problem easier to search by focusing on larger steps. However, a subgoal search may miss a solution even when one exists. This paper introduces complete subgoal search, a way to augment that high-level planning with a completeness guarantee in discrete action spaces.

The method incorporates low-level actions into the high-level search, creating a hybrid search across multiple levels. This retains the practical efficiency offered by subgoals while drawing on low-level search for completeness. The key change is to expand the routes the search can consider, so its ability to find a solution does not depend entirely on the learned subgoals.

The authors apply the method to an existing subgoal search algorithm trained on offline data and evaluate it on complex planning problems. Beyond the completeness guarantee, they find that the hybrid approach can reduce search expansions even on instances already solvable by high-level search alone. The result makes subgoal planning applicable to settings where finding an existing solution is a critical requirement.
neurips-2023-hybrid-search-for-efficient.tldr: Adding low-level actions to subgoal search guarantees completeness in discrete action spaces and can also reduce search expansions.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning policies can earn similar rewards while behaving very differently. This paper studies how to discover many such strategies without sacrificing reward optimization. It identifies a weakness in existing diversity measures: policies that appear visually indistinguishable can still receive high diversity scores, weakening the connection between the metric and meaningful behavior.

The authors incorporate distances between states into the diversity measure to better reflect behavioral differences. They also compare population-based training with iterative learning. Although population-based training gives the precise problem formulation, iterative learning can reach comparable diversity scores more efficiently, allowing better practical solutions with the available computation.

Combining iterative learning with two tractable versions of the state-distance measures produces State-based Intrinsic-reward Policy Optimization, or SIPO. The algorithm has provable convergence properties. Across three experimental domains spanning robot locomotion and multi-agent games, it consistently finds strategically diverse, human-interpretable policies that the evaluated baselines do not discover. The contribution links a more behaviorally meaningful measure with an efficient learning procedure.
neurips-2023-iteratively-learn-diverse-s.tldr: SIPO uses state distances and iterative learning to discover meaningful strategy diversity efficiently, with convergence results and supporting experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies linear regression when privacy protection and corrupted training responses must be handled together. Data points are sampled independently from a common distribution, but an adversary may alter a fraction of their response values. Under standard distributional assumptions, the authors provide a method with proven computational and statistical efficiency.

The algorithm modifies differentially private stochastic gradient descent in two central ways. It uses full-batch gradient descent to improve how many samples are needed, and introduces adaptive clipping to provide robustness. These changes address distinct demands: learning efficiently under privacy constraints and preventing adversarially corrupted responses from undermining the regression procedure.

The method runs in time linear in the input size. Its sample complexity matches the information-theoretic optimum up to a condition-number factor that depends on the data distribution. Thus, the statistical guarantee retains an explicit distribution-dependent qualification. Applied without adversarial corruption, the same algorithm also improves on prior state-of-the-art results and achieves near-optimal sample complexity. The contribution covers both corrupted and uncorrupted private regression settings.
neurips-2023-label-robust-and-differenti.tldr: A private regression algorithm combines full-batch updates and adaptive clipping to achieve efficient learning despite adversarial response corruption.

paragraphs: Evaluating a generated image requires checking how well its content follows the text that requested it. A single image-text matching score can miss object-level composition, contributing to disagreement with human judgments. LLMScore addresses this by evaluating alignment at multiple levels of detail and producing a rationale alongside the score.

The framework first converts the image into descriptions covering both the overall scene and individual objects. It then supplies an evaluation instruction to a large language model, which uses these descriptions to assess alignment with the original text. This creates a language-based evaluation process that explicitly includes both broad image content and more detailed composition.

Across the datasets studied, the authors report the highest correlation with human judgments among the evaluated approaches. LLMScore’s Kendall’s tau correlation is 58.8% higher than CLIP’s and 31.2% higher than BLIP’s in the reported comparisons. These are improvements in agreement with human evaluations, rather than improvements to the generated images themselves. The contribution is an evaluation framework that combines a numerical assessment with an accompanying explanation.
neurips-2023-llmscore-unveiling-the-powe.tldr: LLMScore uses scene and object descriptions to generate image-text alignment scores and rationales that correlate more closely with human judgments in evaluations.

paragraphs: When data arrive continuously, clustering the most recent observations can be more useful than clustering the entire history. The sliding-window model captures this by expiring older points while limiting storage. This paper gives an algorithm for general (k,z)-clustering in that model with a near-optimal approximation guarantee.

The algorithm achieves a (1+ε)-approximation, meaning its clustering objective stays within that multiplicative factor of the optimum. For points in the specified discrete coordinate domain, its space bound scales with k, an accuracy-dependent factor, and polylogarithmic terms. A key ingredient is an online coreset: a sampled summary that supports clustering for every prefix of the stream, rather than only its final state.

The authors also prove a lower bound on the samples required by any online coreset. This establishes that constructing summaries valid across stream prefixes is strictly harder than constructing an offline coreset. The results extend to general metrics on the stated domain, and offline coreset lower bounds support their near-optimality. The paper therefore combines an efficient streaming construction with evidence about the resources such summaries inherently require.
neurips-2023-near-optimal-k-clustering-i.tldr: The paper develops near-optimal sliding-window clustering using online coresets and proves lower bounds on the storage such summaries require.

paragraphs: Some learning problems require a neural field to satisfy specified conditions exactly throughout optimization. This paper develops Constrained Neural Fields, or CNF, to enforce such hard constraints. Its focus is on conditions expressed through linear operators acting on the field and its derivatives, including constraints of arbitrary differential order.

The approaches draw inspiration from meshless interpolation and spectral collocation methods in scientific computing. The authors also design model representations and training strategies for difficulties that arise when networks are constrained. These include numerical conditioning, memory use, and the network’s remaining capacity to represent the desired field while meeting the imposed conditions.

Demonstrations cover a range of real-world applications, and an accompanying framework makes models and constraints efficient to specify. The contribution brings exact constraint satisfaction into the design of neural-field optimization, together with practical strategies for making it workable. Its stated constraint language is central: the conditions are represented as linear operators on the field and its derivatives, providing a concrete mathematical form for the requirements being enforced.
neurips-2023-neural-fields-with-hard-con.tldr: Constrained Neural Fields enforce hard linear-operator constraints on neural fields and their derivatives while addressing practical training difficulties.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents often store past experiences and revisit them during training. Choosing which experiences to replay matters because samples differ in how much they can teach the agent. This paper proposes prioritizing experiences according to observed learning progress, using changes in their training loss over time.

The authors define a sample’s learnability through a steady decline in its associated loss. Their algorithm gives higher priority to samples showing this pattern and lower priority to samples that remain hard to learn, often because of noise or randomness. A large error alone therefore does not establish that repeatedly training on an experience will be productive.

Experiments across multiple domains show greater robustness than random sampling and better results than prioritizing solely by temporal-difference loss, as in prioritized experience replay. The findings support loss reduction as a useful signal for allocating replay effort. The method’s central idea is to distinguish experiences where training is making progress from experiences whose persistent errors may reflect difficulty that further replay does little to resolve.
neurips-2023-prioritizing-samples-in-rei.tldr: Prioritizing replay samples whose losses steadily decrease improves robustness over random sampling and loss-based prioritization in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Grid cells represent location through repeating spatial activity patterns organized into modules with different periods. Mathematical analyses suggest that these multiple periods support high-capacity coding and intrinsic error correction. This paper investigates how such representations can emerge through learning, bringing together insights from dynamical systems, coding theory, function optimization, and supervised deep learning.

The authors construct a self-supervised framework comprising training data, augmentations, loss functions, and a network architecture. It is motivated by the purposes a spatial representation should serve and does not use supervised position information. The method also avoids assuming a particular form for the network’s internal representations or its readout representations.

Networks trained in this framework develop multiple grid-cell modules and generalize substantially beyond their training distribution. The result demonstrates that multi-modular grid representations can emerge under the proposed self-supervised setup. This offers a learning-based perspective on their possible origins and a framework of interest for machine learning. It establishes emergence in the trained networks, without establishing that the same learning process explains biological development.
neurips-2023-self-supervised-learning-of.tldr: A self-supervised spatial learning framework produces multiple grid-cell modules without position labels or prescribed internal representations.

paragraphs: GPS trajectories reveal how people move through cities, but useful datasets can be difficult to access because of privacy concerns, ownership restrictions, and inconsistent quality. SynMob addresses accessibility by creating synthetic trajectories intended to preserve important characteristics of real movement data. The contribution includes both a trajectory-generating system and publicly released datasets.

The synthesizer uses a diffusion model to emulate spatial and temporal behavior in the original trajectories. Its goal is for generated data to retain geographic distributions and statistical properties characteristic of real datasets. These properties matter because urban mobility analysis depends on patterns across locations and time, rather than simply on producing plausible-looking individual routes.

Analyses and case studies find high similarity and useful correspondence between the synthetic data and real-world counterparts. These results support using synthetic trajectories for urban mobility analysis in the settings examined. By releasing the synthesizer alongside the data, the authors also provide a basis for further synthetic dataset creation. The reported evidence concerns fidelity and analytical utility, rather than a formal privacy guarantee.
neurips-2023-synmob-creating-high-fideli.tldr: SynMob uses a diffusion model to generate publicly available synthetic GPS trajectories with demonstrated similarity and utility for urban mobility analysis.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent can use a world model to consider possible actions before acting in its environment. Thinker makes those interactions part of what the agent learns. It wraps the environment with a learned world model and introduces additional actions specifically for interacting with that model.

Through these actions, the agent proposes alternative plans before selecting a final action to execute in the environment. This removes the need to supply a handcrafted planning algorithm: the agent learns how to use the model for planning. The resulting planning activity can also be visualized, making the agent’s considered plans easier to interpret.

Experiments show state-of-the-art performance in Sokoban and competitive results on the Atari 2600 benchmark. Visualizations indicate that trained agents learn to use the world model effectively when selecting actions. The authors identify this as the first demonstration of an RL agent learning to plan with a learned world model in complex environments. The central contribution is making planning behavior itself learnable through the agent’s action interface.
neurips-2023-thinker-learning-to-plan-an.tldr: Thinker gives reinforcement learning agents actions for interacting with a learned world model, enabling them to learn how to plan.

paragraphs: In semi-supervised node classification, a graph neural network learns using labels available for only some nodes. This paper identifies label position bias: nodes closer to labeled nodes tend to receive better predictions. The finding points to the placement of supervision within the graph as a source of unequal predictive performance.

The authors introduce the Label Proximity Score to quantify this bias and find that it is closely associated with performance disparities. This supplies a way to study the relationship between a node’s position relative to labeled examples and the model’s accuracy. The metric makes the observed pattern more explicit than an overall accuracy score alone.

To address the bias, the paper proposes an optimization framework that learns a graph structure intended to be unbiased with respect to label position. The framework can be applied to existing GNNs. Extensive experiments show improved performance over the backbone methods and a significant reduction in label position bias. The results support changing graph structure as a way to improve both predictive performance and its distribution across nodes.
neurips-2023-towards-label-position-bias.tldr: The paper measures GNN performance disparities associated with proximity to labeled nodes and learns graph structures that reduce this bias.

paragraphs: A deployed neural network may encounter a changing stream of inputs, and some distribution changes can damage prediction quality. This paper develops a monitoring method that examines windows of incoming data and raises an alarm when it detects a deviation. It addresses both benign changes and maliciously manipulated inputs.

The detector uses selective prediction principles and is derived from a tight coverage generalization bound. That bound is computed using a sample drawn from the underlying source distribution, then used to monitor the network over test windows. This gives the alarm mechanism a statistical foundation tied to the source sample and the network’s behavior.

The reported detection performance matches or exceeds state-of-the-art methods while reducing computation time by five orders of magnitude and lowering space complexity. A central scaling benefit is that each detection avoids the dependence on source-dataset size required by previous methods. This makes monitoring more practical for very large source datasets. The alarms identify distributional deviations associated with potential quality damage; a detected change is not itself a direct measurement of prediction error.
neurips-2023-window-based-distribution-s.tldr: A statistically grounded window-based detector monitors distribution shifts with competitive detection performance and substantially lower computational costs.
